comments.text:
Doctor Mike, 
I am retired now; however, every word you speak says volumes about reality in an ER. Way back in the early 80's, I spent a little over 3 years in a private hospital as the only RT with trauma experience working by myself M-F from 11p to 7a. Mid-sized hospital with approximately 325 beds. Because it was a private hospital, our resources were drastically cut. I can't say how many times I had to pull a double shift because no one else felt comfortable covering the ER or ICU and CCU. But working alone meant I had to cover  everything, including codes on the upper 8 floors. So many trauma nights are permanently etched in my mind. As other night people will say, we worked as a tight knit team. I learned so much, especially from the specialists who were called in. Was a pre-med student, but I ended up changing to outpatient medical social work and spent my career there. I really appreciate your words of wisdom; as they apply today; just as well as they did 43 years ago.
comments.author: @Charlielizard

comments.text:
As a former mental health crisis response specialist, THANK YOU for reinforcing the need for talking openly about SI. This is one of the main things you learn in ASIST (Applied SI Intervention Skills Training), and as scary as it can be, it is almost always the correct choice. People are really surprised by how much of a relief it is to just say it out loud, name it, get it out. Once you've done that, there's at least one more person in this world that can help carry that burden, and I was always grateful to anyone who would let me help them lighten that load. As a survivor myself, I just think it's so wonderful to hear someone with your size of platform speaking to this!

I will say, Santos's approach would have definitely felt condescending to me when I needed it, and this is actually something we had to train out of people (that, and the "therapist/social worker tone" that people tend to adopt). I mean, I guess if it's the only way you can get yourself to have the conversation, then it's usually better than avoiding it... but, truly the most effective method is talking to people like they're people, and then, and this is important, doing a lot of listening... because you are NOT trying to talk them out of it. They are going to talk themselves out of it, and you're just there to help them remember how. 

Doing it in an inauthentic way  is a method of distancing yourself from the person (and protecting yourself), when what you're really trying to do is bring them closer to you.
comments.author: @Ciarnyn

comments.text: Dr. Mike's advice to directly ask the person about suicidal ideation applies to family and friends too. Asking someone directly if they’re thinking about suicide does not put the idea in their head. Research shows that it can actually bring them relief because someone has finally acknowledged how bad they’re feeling. If someone opens up to you, listen and validate what they’re going through instead of immediately trying to cheer them up. If someone tells you they’re thinking about suicide, don’t keep it a secret. Connecting them to professional support is the most important thing you can do for them.

comments.text: As someone who previously struggled with ideation, you're right about that approach. A few people tried to relate by telling stories about someone in their own life who had similar problems, and it always came off as insincere, comparative, and like they weren't trying to understand me, but make themselves feel better about not noticing the signs in the person in their own life. Worst of all it comes off like if a doctor does it, they're just filling a checkbox that says yes I checked if this patient is having ideation, and if they were I would have involuntarily hospitalised them. The only thing worse is "you're not thinking about it, are you?" trying to lead you to say you're better than you really are and invalidating your entire emotional existence. It just makes you want to shut down and not respond when health care providers do stuff like that. Especially when they haven't even asked you what's wrong. Ask him how he's doing, how his mental state is, and give him the K10 to fill out because it gives him a way to investigate and understand his mental state, admit the severity and consistency of those feelings without having to say it out loud or feel judged or labeled, and gives the opportunity to distance from the responsibility and emotion of his answers. Then ask him if he's had any of those thoughts. There's a reason those procedures are in place, and it's because they show that the doctor is trying to understand, and not just trying to put you in confinement if you admit to them what you might be thinking about.
comments.author: @lw8882
